New York: Lifting the veil of secrecy on US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) chief John Ratcliffe's visit to Moscow, President Donald Trump hinted Wednesday that he had sent him there as part of his bid to end the Ukraine War. Trump told conservative commentator Glenn Beck in an interview: "We’re working very hard to get that war ended, and frankly, they both want to see it ended at this point." Something might come out of the visit, he added, but downplayed its overall significance. Asked if the visit was about NATO or the threatened Iran-related sanctions, Trump said, “None of the above. He’s there, you know, very sort of semi-routine. I hate to disappoint people." Earlier, Russian President Vladimir Putin's spokesperson Dmitry Peskov confirmed the visit that the US had kept under wraps. It was broken by US media based on flight data about an American military plane flying from the US via Latvia to Moscow and diplomatic motorcades in the Russian capital. Peskov told reporters that the CIA chief did not meet President Putin during the visit but spoke with intelligence officials. He did not give details of what was discussed during the visit "All I can tell you is that there have been contacts via the security services," he said The visit took place as the Ukraine War reached a new phase of intensification, with Russia pummeling Ukraine harder, hitting civilian targets. Ukraine was reported to be running short of anti-missile defence equipment, increasing its vulnerability, after it had appeared to make headway in the war. Trump had asserted during his election campaign that he would end the Ukraine within a day of becoming President, but it has dragged on for four years. Also, on the eve of Ratcliffe's visit, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned countries doing business with Iran that they would face serious consequences. Trump had threatened an "Economic D-Day" against Iran, an image that recalls the massive military surge against Nazi Germany that led to the end of World War II. Russia is one of the countries with significant ties to Iran. Some reports said that Russia was helping Iran with intelligence to help it in its confrontation with the US, but Trump has denied it. Peskov also tried to play down the visit's significance, saying: "These contacts often continue even during the most difficult periods in bilateral relations." "It is still too early to say to what extent this will, overall, help to steer our bilateral relations out of the profound crisis in which they currently find themselves", he added. This was Ratcliffe's first visit as CIA chief to Russia.

https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/18/thre.text: Three people are dead after a school shooting in the southern Philippines, including two 14-year-old students and the 16-year-old gunman. At least eight others are reported to be injured.Authorities say the gunman, a student at Banga National High School in South Cotabato, opened fire on students in a neighbouring classroom.The school is located in the town of Banga, which is on the island of Mindanao.This is the third school shooting incident in the Philippines since June.The Governor of South Cotabato, Reynaldo Tamayo, said the two students killed were a boy and a girl. He added the gunman, also shot himself and died.Officials say the teenager had warned friends after lunch that he was “going to do something” and told them to go home, but they thought he was joking.The weapon used in the attack, believed to be a 9mm gun, reportedly belonged to the shooter’s father, a Department of Education employee, and had been stored in a locked vault.The Mayor of Banga, Albert Palencia, told local media that police found posts made by the shooter in an online community, where young people involved in school shootings are "idolized". Quoting the boy's school adviser, Palencia said the mother of the boy wanted to bring him to a psychiatrist.

REUTERS/Kuba Stezycki By Robert Harvey, Marek Strzelecki and Jonathan Saul LONDON/WARSAW, Sept 15 (Reuters) - Saudi Arabia has cut oil shipments to Europe after drone attacks damaged its key export pipeline to the Red Sea, trade sources told Reuters, prompting top customers such as Poland to rush ‌to seek alternatives as cargo prices topped $120 a barrel. The attacks, which Saudi Arabia has blamed on Iraqi militia, forced the kingdom ‌on Friday to shut its East-West desert oil pipeline, which has spared it from the worst of the impact of the closure of the Strait of Hormuz over the last six ​months. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Oil trading and shipping sources said on Tuesday that Saudi Arabia had informed European customers that some September-loading crude cargoes will be cancelled and oil loadings at the Red Sea port of Yanbu had been suspended. State oil company Saudi Aramco declined to comment. The cut in Saudi flows through the Red Sea will prompt Saudi Arabia to try to export more oil via the Strait of Hormuz using so-called dark shipments similar to those already used by the United Arab ‌Emirates and Iraq, trading sources said. Such shipments have allowed ⁠Gulf oil producers to export 7 million to 9 million barrels per day, which is 30% to 40% of pre-war volumes. Advertisement Advertisement The supply disruption supported oil prices, with Brent oil futures trading near $108 a barrel and cargo prices in ⁠Europe's physical market even higher, with key benchmark dated Brent at around $122 per barrel, LSEG data showed. Saudi Arabia loaded 22 million barrels of oil across 12 vessels at Ras Tanura/ Juaymah in the week of September 7 to 13, as opposed to 6 to 7 vessels per week for the prior three weeks, data from ​Vortexa ​showed. Reuters could not immediately determine how many cargoes to Europe would be cancelled or ​for how long Yanbu loadings would be suspended. POLAND'S ORLEN RUSHES TO FIND ‌ALTERNATIVES, TRADERS SAY Advertisement Advertisement Polish integrated oil firm Orlen PKN.WA was rushing to find crude oil cargoes from the North Sea and further afield to replace disrupted Saudi imports, five industry sources said. Aramco became Orlen's top supplier in 2022 and now supplies around 40% of its oil, helping wean it off Russian oil but making it reliant on the Saudi producer. Orlen declined to comment on details of specific commercial transactions, but said it actively manages its supply portfolio to ensure the uninterrupted operation of its refining assets. "Adjusting and optimising purchase volumes is a standard, ongoing part of the Orlen Group's operations, driven by both current production ‌needs and changing market conditions," an Orlen spokesperson told Reuters. Advertisement Advertisement Orlen purchased several cargoes of ​crude oil in spot tenders on Friday and Monday, the sources said. It picked ​up North Sea grades including Grane, Johan Sverdrup and Johan Castberg, ​two said. It also tendered for grades further afield including U.S. WTI Midland and Kazakh CPC Blend, two sources added. It ‌issued another tender on Tuesday to buy North Sea or ​Algerian crude for October delivery and ​Guyanese crude for November delivery, one trader said, but results were slow to surface. Orlen and subsidiaries operate oil refineries in Poland, Lithuania, and the Czech Republic. The Baltic port of Gdansk in Poland received around 160,000 bpd of Saudi crude this year to date, and Lithuania's Butinge ​received 63,000 bpd, data from analytics firm Kpler ‌showed. https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: Student protesters in Place de la République, Paris, on Monday. Photograph: Mohammed Badra/EPA View image in fullscreen Student protesters in Place de la République, Paris, on Monday. Photograph: Mohammed Badra/EPA Opinion France ‘Nobody is listening to us’: on the school protest frontline, I heard why France’s students feel disowned Alexander Hurst Fixing the broken education system will be just the start. The biggest challenge for an aloof political class is to finally pay attention to an abandoned generation Fri 9 Oct 2026 07.48 EDT Last modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 08.09 EDT Share W hen adolescents protest that the government is failing to uphold their right to an education, and the government’s response is to send in riot police, the government has lost the plot. People outside France may have spent the past week watching the student protests in Paris and other cities, and thought, “Well, France has a long tradition of insurrection” or, “That’s just the French being French.” But the situation that has provoked the high-school walkouts and teenage anger is most likely not one they would immediately associate with the France of their imaginations. In place of its lost plot, the French government has a collection of anecdotes and statistics that it should be ashamed of: 27th place in the most recent OECD education rankings , schools with ceilings collapsing and rats in classrooms and, in a school in Bagnolet, no drinkable water ; an increase in the average number of students per class from 27 in 2010 to over 30 today ; half of primary and high schools missing teachers at the start of the school year – many of them with no substitutes or replacements. Julie, a 34-year-old teacher who joined the demonstrations, told me that staff shortages were the fault of “low salaries and poor treatment.” She has to commute for an hour and 45 minutes each way between Paris and the school on the city’s outskirts where she accepted a post last year after switching careers. All for €2100 (£1,780) a month, plus some overtime pay. Teachers’ salaries in France are only 56% of what they are in Germany – even as over €200bn in public subsidies finds its way annually to businesses. So it could easily have been a teacher-led revolt – instead, the high-schoolers themselves cracked first. They paid a high price for refusing to accept a failing education system: a 16-year-old has lost the use of an eye, a 15-year-old has lost a hand, a 14-year-old has a broken jaw – all from police munitions. Hundreds more have been injured in some way. In total, 4,400 people, the vast majority minors, have been arrested in a little over a week, almost half the number of arrests made during the months of gilets jaunes chaos. It might be incoherent that protesting students shoot fireworks at high school buildings, while at the same time denouncing the poor facilities they have to study in. But the far greater incoherence belongs to a government that has disinvested in its youth, and has chosen to answer bin fires with police charges. “Sure some people were burning trash cans,” Fatoumata Sylla Wague, a 17-year-old in her final year at the Lycée Paul Éluard in Seine-Saint-Denis, where pupils were among the first to set up blockades outside their campus, told me. “But trash cans can’t feel anything.” She and her fellow students, on the other hand, certainly felt the teargas that the police launched in response. Despite “unlivable” temperatures in the school buildings, extreme heat and extreme cold, walls covered in mould, electricity cuts and often not enough tables or chairs for everyone, Fatoumata would rather have been in class than out braving the riot police. But she wants to teach history some day and felt compelled, in a moment in history, comparable to May 1968, to take part. “If I’m fighting for our rights today, it’s because I really want to teach, but in good conditions. And so this is for the next generation of students and teachers.” View image in fullscreen Students gather during a blockade at the Lycee Paul-Eluard high school in the northern Paris suburb of Saint-Denis Photograph: Luc Auffret/Anadolu/Getty Images I can’t imagine how hard it must be to be a teenager in general today. In 2021 The Lancet found that 75% of French 16-25-year-olds exhibited signs of eco-anxiety, telling researchers they were “frightened” about the future. In France and beyond, students and young workers actively dislike AI and feel pessimistic about the future it portends. As for Fatoumata, she worries about the rise of far-right political movements, both in France and elsewhere. For years, successive French governments have dealt with problems in some of France’s most troubled urban areas by unleashing heavy-handed policing that all too frequently targets young people with random checks that can be personally degrading. Centralised policymaking has also produced a national education system that often sends its least experienced teachers to these same areas, while granting more senior teachers priority in requesting transfers to other, less difficult, schools. A future far-right government, the kind Fatoumata says she worries about, would almost certainly ramp up these kinds of tensions. Already, in response to the protests, rightwing politicians have called for harsher sentences and more law and order . But this is not a problem that will be solved with more police and more batons, any more than it already has been. Because none of it signals a government that truly wants to listen – it signals that society at large does not really claim these places, or these teenagers, as its own. On n’est pas mal éduqué, on n’est pas écouté (“We’re not poorly educated, we’re just not being listened to”), read one sign I saw brandished at Paris’s Place de la République on Tuesday. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion Responding to the crisis is going to require some tangible acts, such as upgrading dilapidated facilities. Arnaud Richards, 50, head of student services at Iqbal Masih middle school in Saint-Denis, offered me the example of how thoughtful architecture can have more impact than one might expect. The technical high school he previously worked in – Gabriel Péri, in an extremely poor area – reopened in 2022 after a total reconstruction , which, according to Richards, led to a calmer climate for both students and teachers. “Having the school itself be a beautiful place made the community feel more respected,” he told me. That in turn “created a calmer environment” for both students and staff. But a real answer doesn’t stop with better facilities. Showing up to cut ribbons on new construction, or renovations, isn’t enough. During Emmanuel Macron’s decade in power, his government has, on any number of issues, successively failed to listen in a way that makes people feel deeply seen and heard. As Fatoumata said: “Honestly, I don’t think the government cares, they just want to shut us up with false promises. We know nothing will change, because the government doesn’t listen to us.” Of all the things going wrong for France at the moment, this underlying lack of a feeling of “togetherness”, the feeling that nobody is really listening, is going to be the most difficult to deal with. Alexander Hurst writes for Guardian Europe from Paris. https://www.portfolio.hu/global/20261111.text: A miniszter biztonságával kapcsolatos aggodalmak azután erősödtek fel, hogy a Wall Street Journal még 2025 januárjában közölt egy légi felvételt a politikus frissen vásárolt, 12,5 millió dolláros georgetowni villájáról. Egy névtelenséget kérő forrás szerint a fotó alapján pontosan be lehetett azonosítani az ingatlan földrajzi helyzetét, ami végül a költözéshez vezetett. A miniszter környezetéből felelősségteljesebb tájékoztatásra szólították fel a sajtót a közjogi méltóságokat érő fenyegetések közepette. Bessent azért került a célkeresztbe, mert a katonai műveletek mellett ő irányítja az augusztusban indított, Irán teljes pénzügyi és gazdasági elszigetelését célzó kampányt. A pénzügyminisztérium szóvivője hangsúlyozta, hogy a tárcavezetőt nem tántorítják el a fenyegetések, és továbbra is elkötelezett a szankciók, valamint a tengeri blokád fenntartása mellett, amelyek együttesen már az összeomlás szélére sodorták az iráni gazdaságot. A miniszter védelmét szolgáló biztonsági intézkedésekkel egy időben az amerikai igazságügyi minisztérium terrorizmus miatt emelt vádat három iráni állampolgár ellen, akiket közel húsz európai és egyesült államokbeli támadással, illetve merényletkísérlettel hoztak összefüggésbe . A vád szerint közük volt ahhoz a szeptemberi akcióhoz is, amelyet az amerikai katonákat és stratégiai bombázókat állomásoztató angliai Fairford légitámaszpont ellen kíséreltek meg. Az ügyben – amely miatt öt férfit vettek őrizetbe – Andy Burnham brit miniszterelnök október elején nyíltan Iránt tette felelőssé, amit Abbász Aragcsi iráni külügyminiszter határozottan visszautasított. A fenyegetések komolyságát jelzi, hogy az Egyesült Államok hétfőn egy másik angliai brit légibázisról is kimenekítette a repülőgépeit. A katonai feszültség ellenére Marco Rubio amerikai külügyminiszter felvetette, hogy a fegyveres fellépésre talán nem is lesz szükség, ha a gazdasági szankciók és a tengeri blokád elérik céljukat. Donald Trump elnök a közösségi médiában arról írt, hogy az Öböl menti arab államok a jelenlegi állapot, vagyis a blokád fenntartását részesítik előnyben, a háború lezárásához pedig hosszú távú megoldásra és a térségbeli szövetségesek biztonságának garantálására van szükség. Teherán ugyanakkor tagadja, hogy tárgyalások folynának a felek között, Mohszen Rezai iráni biztonsági vezető szerint ugyanis az erről szóló híresztelések csupán a gazdasági nyomás enyhítését és az olajárak letörését szolgálják.
